summary: A country in the west of the Iberian Peninsula that opened sea routes to India and Brazil during the Age of Discovery and built a colonial empire spanning the continents; it is known for fado music and azulejo tile art.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Christianity reached the Iberian Peninsula in the Roman period; after the Muslim conquest of the 8th century, the Christian kingdoms of the north launched the 'Reconquista', and in 1139 Afonso I proclaimed himself king after the Battle of Ourique against the Moors, and the Kingdom of Portugal has been Catholic ever since. The expulsion of the Jews in 1496 and the establishment of the Inquisition in 1536 gave Catholicism a long monopoly over religious life. The apparitions of Our Lady of Fátima in 1917 and the slogan 'God, Fatherland, Family' of the Salazar dictatorship (1932–1968) further strengthened Catholicism's position, and today about eighty percent of the population still identify as Catholic.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: After the Carnation Revolution of 1974 overthrew the dictatorship, Portugal moved toward democracy and secularization, and the 1976 constitution established the separation of church and state. Economic development after joining the European Communities in 1986, the spread of education and urbanization markedly reduced church attendance among young people. The non-religious population is concentrated in large cities such as Lisbon and Porto, and in the southern Alentejo region, which has traditionally been anticlerical and left-wing.

ranking.name: Other Christian (Protestant, Evangelical, etc.)
ranking.description: Protestantism arrived in the 19th century with British merchants, and the wine-trading community of Porto had an Anglican church. In the late 20th century, especially after democratization in 1974, evangelical and Pentecostal churches from Brazil (such as the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God) expanded rapidly because they use the same language, with followers mostly Brazilian immigrants and low- and middle-income urban groups.

ranking.name: Other religions
ranking.description: Other religions include Islam, Hinduism and Judaism. Islam and Hinduism arrived mainly with immigrants from the former colonies of Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau around 1975, and more recently with immigrants from South Asia. In 2015 Portugal passed a law allowing descendants of the Sephardic Jews expelled in 1496 to apply for citizenship.

religion.background: Portugal accepted Christianity in the Roman period; from the 8th to the 13th century parts of it were ruled by Muslims, and after the founding of the kingdom in 1139 Catholicism was the core of its identity. The Jews were expelled in 1496, and the Inquisition was established in 1536. In the Age of Discovery, missionaries traveled with the Portuguese fleets and spread Catholicism to Brazil, Africa and Asia. In the 20th century the Salazar dictatorship was closely tied to the Church; after the Carnation Revolution of 1974 the country moved toward separation of church and state and secularization, but Catholicism remains the cultural identity of the majority.

language.official: The official language is Portuguese, and Mirandese also has official recognition locally.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: Portuguese descends from the vulgar Latin of the northwest of the Iberian Peninsula in the Roman period, and in the Middle Ages was the same language as Galician (Galician-Portuguese). In 1290 King Denis decreed that Portuguese replace Latin as the language of official documents, and founded a university in Lisbon. In the 16th century Camões's epic The Lusiads established the standard of modern Portuguese. Because Portugal is one of the earliest countries in Europe to have fixed its borders, the language is highly uniform, and almost the whole country speaks Portuguese as its mother tongue.

ranking.name: Mirandese
ranking.description: Mirandese is the language of the area around Miranda do Douro in the northeast and belongs to the Asturleonese branch, descending from the language of the medieval Kingdom of León. Because of its remote location and bordering Spain, it has survived locally. In 1999 the Portuguese parliament passed a law recognizing Mirandese, the only official regional language in Portugal, but it has only a few thousand speakers and is in danger of disappearing.

language.history: Portuguese descends from the vulgar Latin of the northwest of the Iberian Peninsula and was influenced by Germanic and Arabic vocabulary. Portugal was founded in the 12th century, and in 1290 King Denis made Portuguese the official language. In the Age of Discovery of the 15th and 16th centuries, Portuguese spread with colonization to Brazil, Africa and Asia, and today it is spoken by more than two hundred million people worldwide. In 1990 the Portuguese-speaking countries signed the Orthographic Agreement in an attempt to unify Portuguese and Brazilian spelling.

ranking.name: Bacalhau (salt cod dishes)
ranking.description: Salted dried cod is soaked in water for one to two days to remove the saltiness, then cooked in many ways, such as stewing, grilling, frying or making into fried cod fritters, with a firm, delicious texture.
ranking.history: Cod is not a fish of Portugal's nearby waters; in the 15th and 16th centuries Portuguese fishermen traveled to the waters off Newfoundland to catch cod, preserving it with salt and bringing it back, so it keeps for a long time and suited ocean voyages and the Catholic meatless days of Lent. In the 20th century the Salazar regime organized the 'White Fleet' to fish for cod off Newfoundland and Greenland. The Portuguese eat large amounts of salt cod each year, and the main dish of Christmas Eve dinner is boiled salt cod with potatoes and cabbage.

ranking.name: Pastel de nata (Portuguese custard tart)
ranking.description: A custard filling of egg yolks, sugar and milk is held in a crisp, multi-layered puff pastry shell and baked at high heat until the surface caramelizes, then eaten sprinkled with cinnamon and powdered sugar.
ranking.history: The pastel de nata originated at the Jerónimos Monastery in Belém, Lisbon, where monks and nuns used egg whites to starch clothes and were left with large quantities of egg yolks, which they used to make sweets. After the monastery was closed following the Liberal Revolution of the 1820s, a sugar refinery nearby began selling these tarts in 1837, which became today's famous Pastéis de Belém, whose recipe is still kept secret. After 1999 it spread through Macau to Hong Kong and Taiwan and became popular in Chinese regions.

ranking.name: Caldo verde (kale soup)
ranking.description: A thick soup base is made from potatoes and onions, then very finely shredded kale is added, topped with a slice of spicy sausage and drizzled with olive oil, giving a light, warming flavor.
ranking.history: Caldo verde originated in the Minho region of northern Portugal, where it is a daily soup of the cold winter in rural areas, with cheap ingredients and simple preparation. Kale grows vigorously in the humid climate of northern Portugal. It is an essential dish at summer folk festivals such as the feast of Saint Anthony and as a late-night snack after wedding banquets, and in 2011 it was voted one of the 'Seven Wonders of Portuguese Gastronomy'.

ranking.name: Francesinha
ranking.description: Toast is filled with several meats such as ham, sausage and steak, covered with melted cheese slices, and drenched in a hot sauce made from beer, tomato and chili, often served with fries.
ranking.history: The francesinha originated in Porto; it is generally thought that in the mid-20th century Daniel da Silva, an emigrant returning from France and Belgium, adapted it from the French croque monsieur and named it after Frenchwomen. It is the most representative dish of Porto, and locals often enjoy it with beer while watching football matches; every restaurant's sauce recipe is a secret.

ranking.name: Cozido à portuguesa (Portuguese boiled stew)
ranking.description: Beef, pork, chicken, blood sausage and smoked sausage are stewed together with vegetables such as cabbage, carrots, potatoes and turnips; the meat and vegetables are served on separate plates, and the broth is eaten separately.
ranking.history: Cozido à portuguesa originated in medieval rural areas, where farmers in winter, after slaughtering pigs, stewed various meats together with vegetables to make full use of every part. In Furnas on the Azores, the volcanic geothermal heat is even used to bury the stew pot underground and cook it slowly for several hours. It is a classic big-pot dish for Sunday family meals and winter gatherings, and is regarded as representative of Portuguese rural food traditions.
